title: ICE-EM Mathematics 10A — Chapter 6: Surface area and volume

classification.difficultyReason: Ten supplied solids require familiar exposed-face decomposition, cut-cylinder fractions, Pythagoras and equal-step inference; the target and representations are supplied, without a new general model or proof.

content.prompt: Calculate the surface area of each solid. Give exact answers, or round non-exact decimal answers to one decimal place.

spec.description: Rectangular prism with dashed hidden edges; ordinary source colours mapped to black.
spec.mathematics: Length 9 cm, depth 6 cm, height 7 cm.

answer.worked:
Opposite faces have equal areas.
$$\begin{align*}S&=2(9\times6)+2(9\times7)+2(6\times7)\\S&=108+126+84\\S&=318\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Long rectangular prism with dashed hidden edges.
spec.mathematics: Length 20 cm, depth 6 cm, height 4 cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}S&=2(20\times6)+2(20\times4)+2(6\times4)\\S&=240+160+48\\S&=448\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Closed cylinder with marked circular centres and full-diameter dimension arrow.
spec.mathematics: Diameter 12 cm, height 10 cm; rear bottom semicircle hidden.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}r&=12\div2=6\text{ cm}\\A_{\text{curved}}&=2\pi\times6\times10\\A_{\text{curved}}&=120\pi\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{end}}&=\pi\times6^2=36\pi\text{ cm}^2\\S&=120\pi+2(36\pi)\\S&=192\pi\text{ cm}^2\\S&\approx603.2\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Half-cylinder with flat rectangular top, semicircular ends, centres and hidden rear end boundary.
spec.mathematics: End diameter 6 cm; longitudinal length 9 cm.

answer.worked:
The two semicircular ends together make one circle; include the flat top.
$$\begin{align*}r&=6\div2=3\text{ cm}\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\tfrac12(2\pi\times3\times9)=27\pi\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{ends}}&=\pi\times3^2=9\pi\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{top}}&=6\times9=54\text{ cm}^2\\S&=27\pi+9\pi+54\\S&=(54+36\pi)\text{ cm}^2\\S&\approx167.1\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Upright right-triangular prism with corresponding right-angle marks and dashed hidden lower edges.
spec.mathematics: Perpendicular triangular sides 9 cm and 40 cm; prism length 42 cm.

answer.worked:
Let the third side of the triangular end be $x$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=9^2+40^2\\x^2&=1681\\x&=41\text{ cm}\\A_{\text{triangle}}&=\tfrac12\times9\times40=180\text{ cm}^2\\S&=2(180)+9\times42+40\times42+41\times42\\S&=360+378+1680+1722\\S&=4140\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Quarter-cylinder with equal perpendicular top radii, matching ticks, right-angle marks and centre points.
spec.mathematics: Radius 5 m; height 10 m; two radial rectangular faces are exposed.

answer.worked:
Include two quarter-circle ends, the curved face and two radial rectangles.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{ends}}&=2\times\tfrac14\pi\times5^2=12.5\pi\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\tfrac14(2\pi\times5\times10)=25\pi\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=2\times5\times10=100\text{ m}^2\\S&=12.5\pi+25\pi+100\\S&=(100+37.5\pi)\text{ m}^2\\S&\approx217.8\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: L-shaped prism with equal horizontal widths marked twice and equal vertical step heights marked once.
spec.mathematics: Front width 20 cm; total height 12 cm; prism length 10 cm. Two step widths equal and two step heights equal.
spec.answerVisibility: Derived 10 cm step widths and 6 cm step heights are omitted.

answer.short:
$1000\text{ cm}^2$

Add the two L-shaped ends and the six rectangular faces.
answer.worked:
The equal step widths are $20\div2=10$ cm; the equal step heights are $12\div2=6$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{end}}&=20\times6+10\times6\\A_{\text{end}}&=180\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=(20+6+10+6+10+12)\times10\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=640\text{ cm}^2\\S&=2(180)+640\\S&=1000\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right-trapezoidal prism with a marked perpendicular corner and dashed hidden edges.
spec.mathematics: Parallel sides 13 and 18 cm; height 12 cm; sloping side 13 cm; prism length 4 cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A_{\text{trapezium}}&=\tfrac12(13+18)\times12\\A_{\text{trapezium}}&=186\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=(13+18+12+13)\times4\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=224\text{ cm}^2\\S&=2(186)+224\\S&=596\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Low trapezoidal prism with interior perpendicular height arrow, separate base label and three double-ticked 5 cm edges.
spec.mathematics: Cross-section bases 13 cm and 5 cm, height 3 cm, one sloping side 5 cm; prism length 5 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Derived other sloping side is not supplied.

answer.short:
$194\text{ cm}^2$

Use Pythagoras to find the other sloping side, then add all face areas.
answer.worked:
The horizontal offset beside the given sloping side is $x$. The other offset is $y$ and its sloping side is $s$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=5^2-3^2=16\\x&=4\text{ cm}\\y&=13-5-4=4\text{ cm}\\s^2&=4^2+3^2=25\\s&=5\text{ cm}\\A_{\text{trapezium}}&=\tfrac12(13+5)\times3=27\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{rectangles}}&=(13+5+5+5)\times5=140\text{ cm}^2\\S&=2(27)+140\\S&=194\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Upright triangular prism with equal perpendicular top sides, double ticks and a right-angle marker.
spec.mathematics: Perpendicular sides both 8 cm; prism length 5 cm.

answer.worked:
Let the third side of the triangular end be $x$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2&=8^2+8^2=128\\x&=8\sqrt2\text{ cm}\\A_{\text{triangle}}&=\tfrac12\times8\times8=32\text{ cm}^2\\S&=2(32)+8\times5+8\times5+8\sqrt2\times5\\S&=(144+40\sqrt2)\text{ cm}^2\\S&\approx200.6\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Find an equilateral triangle's altitude using Pythagoras, then sum the areas of two triangular and three rectangular faces.

content.prompt: The base of a right prism of height $12\text{ cm}$ is an equilateral triangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the side length of the triangle is $6\text{ cm}$, use Pythagoras’ theorem to calculate the height of the triangle.

answer.worked:
The perpendicular height bisects the base into two lengths of $3\text{ cm}$. Let the triangle's height be $h$.
$$\begin{align*}h^2+3^2&=6^2\\h^2&=36-9\\h^2&=27\\h&=3\sqrt3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Calculate the surface area of the prism.

answer.short:
$(216+18\sqrt3)\text{ cm}^2$

Add the areas of the two triangular ends and the three rectangular faces.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area of each triangle}&=\frac12\times6\times3\sqrt3\\\text{Area of each triangle}&=9\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area of each rectangle}&=6\times12\\\text{Area of each rectangle}&=72\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\times9\sqrt3+3\times72\\S&=(216+18\sqrt3)\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Works backwards from the total area of six equal square faces to find the cube's side length.

content.prompt: A cube has surface area $486\text{ m}^2$. Find its side length.

answer.worked:
A cube has six equal square faces. Let its side length be $s$ metres.

$$\begin{align*}6s^2&=486\\s^2&=\frac{486}{6}\\s^2&=81\\s&=9\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Find surface area by adding the areas of all faces. A cube has six equal square faces; reverse this calculation and take the positive square root to obtain a length.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The rectangular-prism surface-area teaching and Example 1 support summing face areas. This question applies that method in reverse to a cube.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the radius and curved surface area into the cylinder formula and solve for height.

content.prompt: A cylinder of base radius $8\text{ cm}$ has curved surface area $72\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Find its height.

answer.worked:
The curved surface area is $2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{align*}2\pi\times8\times h&=72\pi\\16\pi h&=72\pi\\h&=\frac{72\pi}{16\pi}\\h&=4.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 4 derives curved surface area as circumference times height, 2πrh. Page 5 demonstrates substitution into this formula.
teachingContext.mappingNote: This question reverses the taught curved-surface calculation to find height. The cylinder surface-area skill is the closest supplied catalogue match.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows Exercise 6A question 4 with radius 8 cm and curved surface area 72π cm². The teacher image lists Exercise 6A question 4 as 4.5 cm, agreeing with the independent calculation 72π ÷ (2π × 8).

classification.difficultyReason: Selects the surfaces of an open cylinder and rearranges the curved surface area formula to find height.

content.prompt: A rubbish bin is in the shape of an open cylinder.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the bin has radius $15\text{ cm}$ and height $40\text{ cm}$, find its total surface area (do not include the lid), correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
The open bin has one circular base and a curved surface.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{curved}}&=2\pi rh\\A_{\text{curved}}&=2\times\pi\times15\times40\\A_{\text{curved}}&=1200\pi\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{base}}&=\pi r^2\\A_{\text{base}}&=\pi\times15^2\\A_{\text{base}}&=225\pi\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}S&=1200\pi+225\pi\\S&=1425\pi\text{ cm}^2\\S&\approx4476.8\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the bin has radius $15\text{ cm}$ and curved surface area $3500\text{ cm}^2$, find the height of the bin, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A_{\text{curved}}&=2\pi rh\\3500&=2\times\pi\times15\times h\\3500&=30\pi h\\h&=\frac{3500}{30\pi}\\h&=\frac{350}{3\pi}\text{ cm}\\h&\approx37.1\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Add the areas of the actual surfaces. Page 4 derives curved surface area as 2πrh; page 5 Example 2 calculates curved and circular areas separately before adding them.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a applies the taught surface-by-surface method with one circular base because the lid is excluded. Part b substitutes the curved area and radius into 2πrh, then uses inverse operations to find height.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image's Exercise 6A question 5a gives 1425π cm² ≈ 4476.8 cm², matching one radius-15 circular base plus the curved surface of height 40. Question 5b gives 350/(3π) cm ≈ 37.1 cm, matching curved area 3500 cm² divided by circumference 30π cm. Both independently calculated results agree.

content.prompt: Calculate the volume of each solid. Give answers involving $\pi$ exactly.

spec.description: Rectangular prism with all three dimensions retained; ordinary edges and concealed dashed edges use black.
spec.mathematics: Length 10 cm, depth 7 cm, height 4 cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=(10\times7)\times4\\V&=280\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Cube with matching single ticks on front width, receding bottom edge and rear vertical edge.
spec.mathematics: Three mutually perpendicular dimensions are each 6 m.
spec.answerVisibility: Only one supplied length and matching ticks.

answer.worked:
The matching ticks show that all three dimensions are $6\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=6\times6\times6\\V&=216\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Right triangular ends joined by longitudinal edges; two source right-angle marks retained.
spec.mathematics: Triangular base 6 m, altitude 4 m, prism length 12 m.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=\left(\frac12\times6\times4\right)\times12\\V&=144\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangular prism with an internal perpendicular altitude in its right-hand end.
spec.mathematics: Length 70 mm, triangle base 40 mm and altitude 20 mm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=\left(\frac12\times40\times20\right)\times70\\V&=28\,000\text{ mm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Cylinder with diameter dimension beneath its base; centre points and concealed rear base arc retained in black.
spec.mathematics: Diameter 10 cm and height 12 cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}r&=10\div2=5\text{ cm}\\V&=\pi r^2h\\V&=\pi\times5^2\times12\\V&=300\pi\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal half-cylinder with open flat cut face above the curved surface, diameter and longitudinal dimensions distinguished.
spec.mathematics: Semicircle diameter 18 cm; length 30 cm.

answer.short:
$1215\pi\text{ cm}^3$

Use half the area of a circle for the cross-section.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}r&=18\div2=9\text{ cm}\\V&=Ah\\V&=\left(\frac12\pi\times9^2\right)\times30\\V&=1215\pi\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Oblique prism with square horizontal base, perpendicular height dimension and two base right-angle marks.
spec.mathematics: Base 24 cm by 24 cm; perpendicular height 40 cm.

answer.worked:
Use the perpendicular height, $40\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=(24\times24)\times40\\V&=23\,040\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Oblique cylinder with base radius and vertical perpendicular height shown separately from sloping sides.
spec.mathematics: Radius 5 cm; perpendicular height 15 cm.

answer.worked:
Use the perpendicular height, $15\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^2h\\V&=\pi\times5^2\times15\\V&=375\pi\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: L-shaped cross-section extruded backwards and right; all five dimensions retained.
spec.mathematics: Overall width 20 cm, height 18 cm, upright width 8 cm, lower arm height 6 cm, extrusion length 15 cm.

answer.short:
$3240\text{ cm}^3$

Split the cross-section into two rectangles.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A&=20\times6+8\times(18-6)\\A&=120+96\\A&=216\text{ cm}^2\\V&=Ah\\V&=216\times15\\V&=3240\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Channel prism with equal shoulder and channel widths shown by double ticks; vertical 3 cm measures floor thickness.
spec.mathematics: Overall width 18 cm, height 6 cm, length 12 cm; three equal front widths; floor thickness 3 cm.

answer.short:
$1080\text{ cm}^3$

Subtract the rectangular channel from the full rectangular cross-section.
answer.worked:
The three marked widths are equal.
$$\begin{align*}w&=18\div3=6\text{ cm}\\d&=6-3=3\text{ cm}\\A&=18\times6-6\times3\\A&=90\text{ cm}^2\\V&=Ah\\V&=90\times12\\V&=1080\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Isosceles trapezoidal prism; equal nonparallel sides, perpendicular cross-section height and longitudinal length retained.
spec.mathematics: Parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm, perpendicular separation 3 cm, length 20 cm.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12(10+6)\times3\\A&=24\text{ cm}^2\\V&=Ah\\V&=24\times20\\V&=480\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Kite prism with 6 cm horizontal diagonal, total 8 cm vertical extent, 15 cm longitudinal edges, paired kite-side ticks, triple longitudinal ticks, concealed edges and four right-angle marks between cross-section and longitudinal edges.
spec.mathematics: Kite cross-section perpendicular diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm; prism length 15 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Only givens, equality marks and source construction lines.

answer.short:
$360\text{ cm}^3$

Use half the product of the kite's diagonals for its cross-sectional area.

spec.description: Front triangle ABC and rear triangle DEF, joined by AD, BE and CF. Matching single ticks identify AB and AC. DE, EF and EB are hidden dashed edges. No right-angle mark is present at A. Ordinary source blue and red edge strokes are rendered in black, preserving dashed visibility.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If $AB=8\text{ cm}$ and $BC=12\text{ cm}$, find the height of $\triangle ABC$, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Since $AB=AC$, the altitude $AM$ bisects $BC$, so $BM=6\text{ cm}$.

$$\begin{align*}AM^2&=AB^2-BM^2\\AM^2&=8^2-6^2\\AM^2&=28\\AM&=\sqrt{28}\\AM&\approx5.29\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $AD=24\text{ cm}$, find the volume of the prism, correct to two decimal places.

answer.short:
$761.98\text{ cm}^3$

Multiply the triangular cross-sectional area by the prism length, retaining the exact height from part a.
answer.worked:
Using the exact triangular height $\sqrt{28}\text{ cm}$ from part a:

$$\begin{align*}V&=Ah\\V&=\left(\frac12\times12\times\sqrt{28}\right)\times24\\V&=288\sqrt7\\V&\approx761.98\text{ cm}^3.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a obtains the triangular altitude using the equal sides and Pythagoras. Part b applies the triangular-prism method of Example 3b using that altitude and AD as the prism length. Supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate the prerequisite Pythagoras step.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply cube volume in reverse using one cube root, exact in the first case and one-decimal rounding in the second. No modelling choice or multi-method inference.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If a cube has volume $64\text{ cm}^3$, find its side length.

answer.worked:
Let $s$ be the side length in centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}s^3&=64\\s&=\sqrt[3]{64}\\s&=4.\end{align*}$$
The side length is $4\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If a cube has volume $400\text{ cm}^3$, find its side length, correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
Let $s$ be the side length in centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}s^3&=400\\s&=\sqrt[3]{400}\\s&\approx7.4.\end{align*}$$
The side length is $7.4\text{ cm}$, correct to one decimal place.

The farmer has 60 horses that each drink about $10\text{ L}$ of water per day. spec.description: Open pentagonal trough extending upwards to the right. The near end consists of a rectangle above a downward-pointing right-angled triangle. answer.short:
$\displaystyle\frac{1500}{2+3\sqrt2}\text{ cm}\approx240.28\text{ cm}$.

Find the pentagonal cross-sectional area, then divide the required volume by this area.
answer.worked:
The required daily capacity is
$$\begin{align*}V&=60\times10\\V&=600\text{ L}\\V&=600\,000\text{ cm}^3.\end{align*}$$
Let $w$ be the width of the rectangular portion. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}w^2&=40^2+40^2\\w^2&=3200\\w&=40\sqrt2\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
The pentagonal cross-section is a rectangle and a right-angled triangle:
$$\begin{align*}A&=30\times40\sqrt2+\frac12\times40\times40\\A&=1200\sqrt2+800\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$
Using $V=A\ell$,
$$\begin{align*}\ell&=\frac{600\,000}{1200\sqrt2+800}\\\ell&=\frac{1500}{2+3\sqrt2}\text{ cm}\\\ell&\approx240.28\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A solid, $A$, is enlarged to form a new solid, $B$. If the surface area of $B$ is twice the surface area of $A$, by what factor is the volume of $A$ multiplied to give the volume of $B$?

answer.short:
$2\sqrt{2}$

The length factor is $\sqrt{2}$, so the volume factor is $(\sqrt{2})^3$.
answer.worked:
Let $k>0$ be the enlargement factor for lengths.
$$\begin{align*}k^2&=2\\k&=\sqrt{2}\\\frac{V_B}{V_A}&=k^3\\\frac{V_B}{V_A}&=(\sqrt{2})^3\\\frac{V_B}{V_A}&=2\sqrt{2}\end{align*}$$

answer.short: The area increases by a factor of 7.
answer.worked:
Let the original base be $b$ and the unchanged height be $h$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{original}}&=\frac12 bh\\A_{\text{new}}&=\frac12(7b)h\\A_{\text{new}}&=7A_{\text{original}}\end{align*}$$
The area increases by a factor of 7.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The sides of the square base of a cube are each increased in length by a factor of 6, but the height is kept the same. This produces a square prism. By what factor has the volume changed?

answer.short: The volume increases by a factor of 36.
answer.worked:
Let the original cube have side length $s$. The new base has side length $6s$, and the height remains $s$.
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{original}}&=s^2\times s\\V_{\text{original}}&=s^3\\V_{\text{new}}&=(6s)^2\times s\\V_{\text{new}}&=36s^3\end{align*}$$
The volume increases by a factor of 36.

answer.short: The volume increases by a factor of 9.

children.prompt: The external surface area of the building is $10\,600\text{ m}^2$. Calculate the external surface area of the model, in $\text{cm}^2$.

answer.worked:
The model's lengths are $\frac{1}{400}$ of the building's lengths, so its surface area is multiplied by $\left(\frac{1}{400}\right)^2$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{model}}&=10\,600\times\left(\frac{1}{400}\right)^2\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{model}}&=0.06625\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{model}}&=0.06625\times100^2\text{ cm}^2\\A_{\text{model}}&=662.5\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The volume of the building is $60\,000\text{ m}^3$. Calculate the volume of the model, in $\text{cm}^3$.

answer.worked:
The model's volume is multiplied by $\left(\frac{1}{400}\right)^3$.
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{model}}&=60\,000\times\left(\frac{1}{400}\right)^3\text{ m}^3\\V_{\text{model}}&=0.0009375\text{ m}^3\\V_{\text{model}}&=0.0009375\times100^3\text{ cm}^3\\V_{\text{model}}&=937.5\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

In the pyramid below, $F$ is the midpoint of $AB$. $VF$ is vertical and is $5\text{ m}$ in length. $ABCD$ is horizontal and rectangular, with $AB=6\text{ m}$ and $BC=8\text{ m}$.

Find:

spec.description: Rectangular-based pyramid with apex vertically above F, the midpoint of rear edge AB. Visible edges VD, VC, VB, DC and CB are solid; hidden edges DA, AB and AV are dashed. The altitude VF is red dashed and has a right-angle marker at F. No face fills.
spec.mathematics: AB=6 m, BC=8 m, AF=FB=3 m and VF=5 m. F lies on AB, not at the centre of the rectangle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source labels and structural givens are visible; no calculated lengths or answers.

children.label: a
children.prompt: the volume of this solid

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}A_{\text{base}}&=6\times8=48\text{ m}^2\\V&=\frac13 A_{\text{base}}h\\V&=\frac13\times48\times5\\V&=80\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the surface area of this solid

inlines.text: Use Pythagoras’ theorem to find the face heights, then add the four triangular faces and the rectangular base.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}AF=FB&=\frac62=3\text{ m}\\VA^2=VB^2&=5^2+3^2=34\\VA=VB&=\sqrt{34}\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
Since $AD$ and $BC$ are perpendicular to the vertical plane $VAB$, $VA$ and $VB$ are the perpendicular heights of faces $VAD$ and $VBC$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{VAD}+A_{VBC}&=2\times\frac12\times8\times\sqrt{34}\\A_{VAD}+A_{VBC}&=8\sqrt{34}\text{ m}^2\\A_{VAB}&=\frac12\times6\times5\\A_{VAB}&=15\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $DC$. Then $FM=8\text{ m}$ and $VM$ is the perpendicular height of face $VDC$.
$$\begin{align*}VM^2&=5^2+8^2=89\\VM&=\sqrt{89}\text{ m}\\A_{VDC}&=\frac12\times6\times\sqrt{89}\\A_{VDC}&=3\sqrt{89}\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{base}}&=6\times8=48\text{ m}^2\\S&=48+15+8\sqrt{34}+3\sqrt{89}\\S&=(63+8\sqrt{34}+3\sqrt{89})\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Find the volume and surface area of the solids.

spec.description: Sector prism with radius 50 mm, sector angle 60 degrees and longitudinal length 200 mm. The rear hidden radius is dashed. Ordinary source blue and red marks are rendered black.
spec.mathematics: Congruent circular-sector ends have radius 50 mm and central angle 60 degrees; prism length is 200 mm.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens only; no calculated lengths, areas or volumes.

answer.short:
$V=\dfrac{250\,000\pi}{3}\text{ mm}^3$, $S=\left(20\,000+\dfrac{12\,500\pi}{3}\right)\text{ mm}^2$.

Use the sector area for each end and include both rectangular cut faces.
answer.worked:
The cross-section is one-sixth of a circle.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{60}{360}\pi(50)^2\\A&=\frac{1250\pi}{3}\text{ mm}^2\\V&=A\times200\\V&=\frac{1250\pi}{3}\times200\\V&=\frac{250\,000\pi}{3}\text{ mm}^3\end{align*}$$
The surface consists of two sector ends, two rectangular faces and the curved face.
$$\begin{align*}L&=\frac{60}{360}\times2\pi\times50\\L&=\frac{50\pi}{3}\text{ mm}\\S&=2\left(\frac{1250\pi}{3}\right)+2(50\times200)+\frac{50\pi}{3}\times200\\S&=\left(20\,000+\frac{12\,500\pi}{3}\right)\text{ mm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Closed hemisphere with both the vertical radius and the horizontal base radius labelled 15 cm; hidden rear base arc dashed. Ordinary source colours are replaced by black.
spec.mathematics: Hemisphere radius 15 cm; total surface includes its circular base.
spec.answerVisibility: Both redundant radius givens remain visible; no answers.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac12\times\frac43\pi r^3\\V&=\frac23\pi(15)^3\\V&=2250\pi\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$
Include the circular base as well as the curved surface.
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\pi r^2+\pi r^2\\S&=3\pi(15)^2\\S&=675\pi\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Cylinder with congruent cones attached above and below. Both join radii are labelled 1 m, cylinder height 3 m and both cone heights 1.5 m. Hidden rear join arcs are dashed; no fill.
spec.mathematics: Common radius 1 m; cylinder height 3 m; each cone perpendicular height 1.5 m. Circular interfaces are internal.
spec.answerVisibility: All five original measurements remain visible; slant height is not supplied.

answer.short:
$V=4\pi\text{ m}^3$, $S=(6+\sqrt{13})\pi\text{ m}^2$.

Add the component volumes; only the curved surfaces are exposed.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^2h+2\left(\frac13\pi r^2H\right)\\V&=\pi(1)^2(3)+2\left(\frac13\pi(1)^2\frac32\right)\\V&=4\pi\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$
For either cone, use Pythagoras' theorem to find its slant height.
$$\begin{align*}\ell^2&=1^2+\left(\frac32\right)^2\\\ell^2&=\frac{13}{4}\\\ell&=\frac{\sqrt{13}}2\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
The circular joins are internal, so only curved surfaces contribute.
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\pi rh+2\pi r\ell\\S&=2\pi(1)(3)+2\pi(1)\frac{\sqrt{13}}2\\S&=(6+\sqrt{13})\pi\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Vertical cylinder capped by two hemispheres. Preserve five separate 5 m labels and the 10 m diameter. Hidden rear join arcs are dashed and dimension extensions dotted.
spec.mathematics: All components share radius 5 m; cylinder height 5 m. The circular joins are internal.
spec.answerVisibility: All six original measurement labels remain visible; no answers.

answer.short:
$V=\dfrac{875\pi}{3}\text{ m}^3$, $S=150\pi\text{ m}^2$.

The two hemispheres together contribute one sphere's volume and curved area.
answer.worked:
The two hemispheres together form a sphere of radius $5\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=\pi r^2h+\frac43\pi r^3\\V&=\pi(5)^2(5)+\frac43\pi(5)^3\\V&=125\pi+\frac{500\pi}{3}\\V&=\frac{875\pi}{3}\text{ m}^3\end{align*}$$
The circular joins are internal.
$$\begin{align*}S&=2\pi rh+4\pi r^2\\S&=2\pi(5)(5)+4\pi(5)^2\\S&=150\pi\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Let the base side be $s$ cm. The perpendicular height is $3s$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}V&=s^2(3s)\\192&=3s^3\\s^3&=64\\s&=4\end{align*}$$
Each side of the base is $4\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: The surface area of a cube is $x\text{ cm}^2$ and its volume is $y\text{ cm}^3$. If $x=y$, find the length of the side of the cube.

answer.worked:
Let the side length be $s$ cm, where $s>0$. Then $x=6s^2$ and $y=s^3$.
$$\begin{align*}6s^2&=s^3\\6&=s\\s&=6\end{align*}$$
The side length is $6\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: A cone has radius $R$, base area $A$ and height $h$. A horizontal slice is taken at a distance $x$ units from the vertex, as shown. Let $A_x$ be the area of the circular slice and $r$ be the radius.

spec.description: Cone with a circular horizontal section, full height h, vertex-to-section distance x, radii r and R, areas A_x and A, axial guide and right-angle marks.
spec.mathematics: A horizontal section parallel to the base creates corresponding axial right triangles with heights x,h and radii r,R. Diagram proportions are illustrative.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels are supplied givens; no ratio or proof is printed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use similar triangles to show that $\dfrac{r}{R}=\dfrac{x}{h}$.

answer.short:
$\dfrac{r}{R}=\dfrac{x}{h}$.

The axial right triangles share the vertex angle, so corresponding sides are proportional.
answer.worked:
Take a vertical section through the cone's axis and the two radii. The smaller and larger right triangles share the angle at the vertex, so they are similar by AA. Their corresponding horizontal sides are $r$ and $R$, and their corresponding vertical sides are $x$ and $h$. Hence
$$\frac{r}{R}=\frac{x}{h}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the ratio $A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

answer.short:
$A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

The area ratio is the square of the corresponding radius ratio.
answer.worked:
The circular areas are $A_x=\pi r^2$ and $A=\pi R^2$. Using part a,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{A_x}{A}&=\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi R^2}\\\frac{A_x}{A}&=\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\\\frac{A_x}{A}&=\frac{x^2}{h^2}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

content.prompt: A square pyramid has base length $2a$, base area $A$ and height $h$. A horizontal slice is taken at a distance $x$ units from the vertex, as shown. Let $A_x$ be the area of the square slice and $2b$ be the side length of the square slice. Use the method of question 4 to show that $A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

spec.description: Square pyramid with parallel square section; the two compared areas retain light blue fill. Ordinary visible and hidden edges use black; perpendicular construction guides retain red.
spec.mathematics: Base side 2a, section side 2b, total perpendicular height h and vertex-to-section distance x; areas A and A_x.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels and construction lines are permanent givens; no answer is drawn.

answer.short:
$A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

Similar triangles give $b/a=x/h$; square this ratio to compare the square areas.
answer.worked:
The triangular sections through corresponding base and slice sides are similar because the slice is parallel to the base.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{2b}{2a}&=\frac{x}{h}\\\frac{b}{a}&=\frac{x}{h}\end{align*}$$

The square areas are $A_x=(2b)^2$ and $A=(2a)^2$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{A_x}{A}&=\frac{(2b)^2}{(2a)^2}\\\frac{A_x}{A}&=\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^2\\\frac{A_x}{A}&=\frac{x^2}{h^2}\end{align*}$$

Hence $A_x:A=x^2:h^2$.

content.prompt: The portion of a right cone remaining after a smaller cone is cut off it is called a frustum. Suppose that the top and bottom are circles of radius $r$ and $R$, respectively. Also, suppose that the height of the frustum is $h$ and the height of the original cone is $H$.

spec.description: Complete original cone retained above and below its horizontal circular cut. Rear arcs are dashed; front arcs and silhouette are solid. No face shading is needed.
spec.mathematics: Original height H, frustum height h, cut radius r and base radius R. The removed cone has height H-h.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the volume $V$ of the frustum is $\dfrac13\pi\left[H(R^2-r^2)+r^2h\right]$.

answer.short:
$V=\dfrac13\pi\left[H(R^2-r^2)+r^2h\right]$.

Subtract the smaller cone, of height $H-h$, from the original cone.
answer.worked:
The removed cone has radius $r$ and height $H-h$.

$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac13\pi R^2H-\frac13\pi r^2(H-h)\\V&=\frac13\pi\left(R^2H-r^2H+r^2h\right)\\V&=\frac13\pi\left[H(R^2-r^2)+r^2h\right]\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use similar triangles to show that $H=\dfrac{hR}{R-r}$.

answer.worked:
The axial triangles of the smaller and original cones are similar.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{r}{R}&=\frac{H-h}{H}\\rH&=R(H-h)\\rH&=RH-Rh\\H(R-r)&=Rh\\H&=\frac{hR}{R-r}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Deduce that $V=\dfrac13\pi h(R^2+r^2+rR)$.

answer.short:
$V=\dfrac13\pi h(R^2+r^2+rR)$.

Substitute part b into part a and use $R^2-r^2=(R-r)(R+r)$.
answer.worked:
Substitute the result of part b into part a.

$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac13\pi\left[\frac{hR}{R-r}(R^2-r^2)+r^2h\right]\\V&=\frac13\pi\left[\frac{hR}{R-r}(R-r)(R+r)+r^2h\right]\\V&=\frac13\pi\left[hR(R+r)+r^2h\right]\\V&=\frac13\pi h(R^2+r^2+rR)\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a general truncated-pyramid formula using similarity and subtraction, then compare volumes.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the method of question 6 to show that the volume of a truncated square pyramid with height $h$ and square base and square top of side lengths $x$ and $y$, respectively, is given by $\frac{1}{3}h(x^2+y^2+xy)$. (A truncated pyramid is formed in a similar way to a frustum.)

answer.short:
$V=\frac{1}{3}h(x^2+y^2+xy)$.

Use similar triangles to relate the heights, then subtract the smaller pyramid from the whole pyramid.
answer.worked:
Let $H$ be the height of the whole pyramid. The removed pyramid has height $H-h$. Corresponding lengths in similar triangles give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{H-h}{H}&=\frac{y}{x}\\xH-xh&=yH\\H(x-y)&=xh\\H&=\frac{xh}{x-y}.\end{align*}$$
Subtract the volume of the removed pyramid:
$$\begin{align*}V&=\frac{1}{3}x^2H-\frac{1}{3}y^2(H-h)\\V&=\frac{1}{3}\left[H(x^2-y^2)+y^2h\right]\\V&=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{xh}{x-y}(x-y)(x+y)+y^2h\right]\\V&=\frac{1}{3}h\left[x(x+y)+y^2\right]\\V&=\frac{1}{3}h(x^2+y^2+xy).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the top square has a side length that is half that of the bottom square, what is the ratio of the volume of the truncated pyramid to that of the whole pyramid?

answer.short:
$7:8$.

The removed pyramid has half the corresponding lengths, so its volume is one-eighth of the whole pyramid.
answer.worked:
The removed pyramid and the whole pyramid are similar, with corresponding side-length ratio $1:2$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{V_{\text{removed}}}{V_{\text{whole}}}&=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3\\\frac{V_{\text{removed}}}{V_{\text{whole}}}&=\frac{1}{8}\\\frac{V_{\text{truncated}}}{V_{\text{whole}}}&=1-\frac{1}{8}\\\frac{V_{\text{truncated}}}{V_{\text{whole}}}&=\frac{7}{8}.\end{align*}$$
The required ratio is $7:8$.

content.prompt: A cone has height $h$ and base radius $r$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the surface area of the cone is $\pi r\left(r+\sqrt{r^2+h^2}\right)$.

answer.short:
$S=\pi r\left(r+\sqrt{r^2+h^2}\right)$.

Use Pythagoras to find the slant height, then add the base and curved surface areas.
answer.worked:
Let the slant height be $\ell$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}\ell^2&=r^2+h^2\\\ell&=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}.\end{align*}$$
The total surface area is
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi r^2+\pi r\ell\\S&=\pi r^2+\pi r\sqrt{r^2+h^2}\\S&=\pi r\left(r+\sqrt{r^2+h^2}\right).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose that the height and radius are equal. Show that the surface area is $\pi r^2(1+\sqrt{2})$.

answer.worked:
Substitute $h=r$ into the result of part a. Since $r>0$,
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi r\left(r+\sqrt{r^2+r^2}\right)\\S&=\pi r\left(r+r\sqrt{2}\right)\\S&=\pi r^2(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{align*}$$

spec.sourceRegion: Question 9, upper-right cone and frustum figure
spec.description: Full cone retained above a horizontal circular cut. Full slant height ℓ, frustum slant height s, radii r and R, perpendicular frustum height h, centre dots and right-angle markers are retained. Ordinary source blue and red marks become black; hidden arcs remain dashed. No decorative fill.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let the slant height of the full cone be $\ell$. Show that $\ell=\dfrac{sR}{R-r}$.

answer.short:
$\ell=\dfrac{sR}{R-r}$.

Use corresponding radius and slant-height ratios in the similar cones.
answer.worked:
The removed cone has radius $r$ and slant height $\ell-s$. The cones are similar, so
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\ell-s}{\ell}&=\frac{r}{R}\\R(\ell-s)&=r\ell\\R\ell-Rs&=r\ell\\\ell(R-r)&=Rs\\\ell&=\frac{sR}{R-r}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, show that the surface area of the curved section is $\pi(r+R)s$, and that the total surface area is $\pi(r^2+R^2)+\pi(r+R)s$.

answer.short:
Curved surface area: $\pi(r+R)s$.

Total surface area: $\pi(r^2+R^2)+\pi(r+R)s$.

Subtract the smaller cone’s curved area from the full cone’s, then add both circular ends.
answer.worked:
Subtract the curved area of the removed cone:
$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{curved}}&=\pi R\ell-\pi r(\ell-s)\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\pi\bigl((R-r)\ell+rs\bigr)\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\pi\left((R-r)\frac{sR}{R-r}+rs\right)\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\pi(Rs+rs)\\A_{\text{curved}}&=\pi(r+R)s.\end{align*}$$
Add the two circular ends:
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi r^2+\pi R^2+A_{\text{curved}}\\S&=\pi(r^2+R^2)+\pi(r+R)s.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the latter can be written as $\pi(r+R)\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}+\pi(r^2+R^2)$, where $h$ is the height of the frustum.

answer.worked:
An axial section gives a right-angled triangle with legs $h$ and $R-r$ and hypotenuse $s$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}s^2&=h^2+(R-r)^2\\s&=\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the total surface area from part b:
$$\begin{align*}S&=\pi(r^2+R^2)+\pi(r+R)s\\S&=\pi(r+R)\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}+\pi(r^2+R^2).\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the radius of the circular cross-section of the sphere at height $h$ is $\sqrt{r^2-h^2}$.

answer.worked:
Let the cross-section radius be $x$. The diagram gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $r$ and legs $h$ and $x$:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+h^2&=r^2\\x^2&=r^2-h^2\\x&=\sqrt{r^2-h^2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Deduce that the area of the cross-section is $\pi(r^2-h^2)$.

answer.worked:
Using the radius from part a,
$$\begin{align*}A&=\pi x^2\\A&=\pi\left(\sqrt{r^2-h^2}\right)^2\\A&=\pi(r^2-h^2).\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Draw a diagram of the cross-section of the cylinder with the cone removed, and show that the area of the cross-section at height $h$ is also $\pi(r^2-h^2)$.

answer.short: An annulus with outer radius $r$ and inner radius $h$; its area is $\pi r^2-\pi h^2=\pi(r^2-h^2)$.
answer.worked:
The cylinder’s section is a circle of radius $r$. The removed cone’s section has radius $h$, as shown in the supplied diagram. The remaining section is an annulus:
$$\begin{align*}A&=A_{\text{outer circle}}-A_{\text{inner circle}}\\A&=\pi r^2-\pi h^2\\A&=\pi(r^2-h^2).\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Complete solution plan view: concentric circles with outer radius r and removed inner radius h. Light blue identifies only the remaining annular section.
spec.mathematics: Remaining area equals πr²−πh².

children.label: d
children.prompt: We now conclude that the two solids have the same volume, by Cavalieri’s principle. Find the volume of the cylinder minus the cone.

answer.worked:
Both the cylinder and the removed cone have base radius $r$ and height $r$:
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{remaining}}&=\pi r^2\times r-\frac13\pi r^2\times r\\V_{\text{remaining}}&=\pi r^3-\frac13\pi r^3\\V_{\text{remaining}}&=\frac23\pi r^3.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Deduce the formula for the volume of the sphere.

answer.short:
$V=\dfrac43\pi r^3$.

A sphere has twice the volume of the hemisphere.
answer.worked:
By Cavalieri’s principle, the hemisphere has volume $\frac23\pi r^3$. A sphere consists of two such hemispheres:
$$\begin{align*}V_{\text{sphere}}&=2\times\frac23\pi r^3\\V_{\text{sphere}}&=\frac43\pi r^3.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$S=4\pi r^2$.

The pyramid volumes sum to $\frac13rS$, which equals the sphere volume $\frac43\pi r^3$.
answer.worked:
Let $S$ be the surface area of the sphere. The small base areas together make up $S$. In the very-small-pyramid model, each pyramid has height $r$, so their total volume is $\frac13rS$.

This equals the volume of the sphere:

entries.description:
In this chapter, we will review and extend the ideas of the surface area and the volume of a solid. Problems involving calculating volume and surface area are very practical and important. Most of the chapter concerns prisms and pyramids, which are the most common polyhedra. We will also see how to find the volume and surface area of solids such as cones, cylinders and spheres.

This chapter contains a number of formulas for volumes and areas.

entries.description:
The prism has six faces.
Area of top rectangle = 12 × 5
= 60 cm²
Area of front rectangle = 12 × 8
= 96 cm²
Area of side rectangle = 8 × 5
= 40 cm²
Thus, S = 2 × 60 + 2 × 96 + 2 × 40
= 392 cm²

entries.description:
We need to find the length AB in the diagram. We can find this using Pythagoras’ theorem.
AB² = 6² + 8²
= 100
so AB = 10 cm
Area of the sloping rectangle = 10 × 20
= 200 cm²
Area of each triangle = ½ × 6 × 8
= 24 cm²
Area of the base rectangle = 6 × 20
= 120 cm²
Area of the back rectangle = 8 × 20
= 160 cm²
Thus, S = 24 + 24 + 120 + 160 + 200
= 528 cm²

entries.description:
Surface area of a cylinder
A cylinder is a solid that has parallel circular discs of equal radius at the top and the bottom. Each cross-section parallel to the base is a circle, and the centres of these circular cross-sections lie on a straight line. If that line is perpendicular to the base, the cylinder is called a right cylinder. When we use the word ‘cylinder’ in this book, we will generally mean a right cylinder.

The right cylinder includes a right-angle marker at the bottom centre.

entries.description:
Surface area of the curved surface
Suppose we have a cylinder with base radius r and height h. If we roll the cylinder along a flat surface through one revolution, as shown in the diagram, the curved surface traces out a rectangle. The width of the rectangle is the height of the cylinder, while the length of the rectangle is the circumference of the circle, which is 2πr, so the area of the curved part is 2πrh. Thus:
Curved surface area of cylinder = 2πrh

entries.description:
Volume of a cylinder
The area of a regular polygon inscribed in a circle approximates the area of that circle. The greater the number of sides, the better the approximation. A cylinder has a circular base. Since V = Ah holds for any polygon-based prism, it seems reasonable that the volume of the cylinder should be the area of its circular base multiplied by the height.
Thus, the volume of a cylinder with radius r and height h is equal to the area of the circular cross-section, πr², multiplied by the height, h.
Volume of a cylinder = πr²h
Cavalieri’s principle shows that this also applies to an oblique cylinder.

entries.description:
Here is a method for determining the formula for the volume of a right, square-based pyramid.
Consider a cube of side length 2x. If we draw the long diagonals as shown, then we obtain 6 square pyramids, one of which is shaded in the diagram. Each of these pyramids has base area 2x × 2x and height x. Let V be the volume of each pyramid.
The volume of the cube is (2x)^3 = 8x^3. Hence:
6 × V = 8x^3
so V = 4/3 × x^3
Now the area of the base of each pyramid is (2x)^2 = 4x^2 and the height of each pyramid is x, so in this case we can write:
V = 4/3 × x^3
  = 1/3 × 4x^2 × x
or V = 1/3 × area of base × height

entries.description:
We need to find the height VE of triangle VBC, using Pythagoras’ theorem.
VE² = VO² + OE²
= 4² + 3²
= 25
Hence, VE = 5 cm.
Area of △VCB = ½ × CB × VE
= ½ × 6 × 5
= 15 cm²
Area of base = 6 × 6
= 36 cm²
Surface area = 4 × 15 + 36
= 96 cm²
Hence, the surface area of the pyramid is 96 cm².

entries.description:
Surface area of a cone
To calculate the surface area of a cone, we need to find the area of each surface. To find the area of the curved surface, we cut and open up the curved surface to form a sector, as shown below.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: Three stages connected by right-pointing arrows: an inverted cone with base radius r and slant height ℓ; the cone cut and partially opened along its curved surface; the flattened curved surface forming a circular sector. The first cone has a red centre dot, a dashed radius and a dashed centre-to-vertex line. The sector has matching tick marks on its two straight radii and an ℓ label.

presentation.orientation: Horizontal left-to-right transformation sequence.

entries.description:
• The arc length of the sector = circumference of the circular base of the cone = 2πr
• The proportion of a whole circle = arc length / whole circumference = 2πr / (2πℓ) = r / ℓ
• Area of sector A = (r / ℓ) × πℓ² = πrℓ
Thus, the surface area of the curved part of a cone is given by:
Curved surface area = πrℓ,
where r is the base radius and ℓ is the slant height.

entries.description: A spherical balloon has radius 10 cm. It is inflated so that the radius becomes 15 cm. By what factor has the following changed?
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone worked example retained as taught-method evidence; excluded from practice-only sections.

presentation.parts: a and b appear side by side beneath the shared stem.

entries.description: surface area
entries.exclusionReason: Part of excluded standalone Example 14.

entries.description: volume
entries.exclusionReason: Part of excluded standalone Example 14.

entries.description:
Method 1 – Find the two areas
For a sphere, A = 4πr²
Hence, surface area of the balloon = 4 × π × 10² = 400π cm²
If the radius becomes 15 cm, then the surface area becomes 4 × π × 15² = 900π cm²,
so the surface area has been multiplied by a factor of 900π/(400π) = 9/4
Method 2 – Enlargement factor method
Enlargement factor for the radius is 15/10 = 3/2.
Hence, enlargement for the surface area is (3/2)² = 9/4.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied working for excluded standalone Example 14; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
Method 1 – Find the two volumes
For a sphere, V = (4/3)πr³.
Hence, volume of the balloon = (4/3) × π × 10³ = (4000/3)π cm³.
If the radius becomes 15 cm, then the volume becomes (4/3) × π × 15³ = 4500π cm³, so the volume has been multiplied by a factor of 4500π ÷ (4000π/3) = 27/8.
Method 2 – Enlargement factor method
The enlargement factor for the radius is 3/2.
Hence, the enlargement factor for the volume is (3/2)³ = 27/8.

entries.description:
Let k > 0.
• If a plane figure is enlarged by a factor of k, then the area of the figure is multiplied by a factor of k^2.
• If a solid is enlarged by a factor of k, then the surface area of the solid is multiplied by a factor of k^2.
• If a solid is enlarged by a factor of k, then the volume of the solid is multiplied by a factor of k^3.

entries.description:
Cavalieri’s principle states that if we have two solids of the same height and the cross-sections of each solid taken at the same distance from the base have the same area, then the solids have the same volume. Take a hemisphere of radius r and look at the area of a typical cross-section at height h above the base.

Also, consider a cylinder of height r and radius r, with a cone cut out of it, also of height r and base radius r. We also take a cross-section at height h.
